EU approval path details
  • RDW (NL) granted FSD (Supervised) a provisional EU type approval under Art. 39(4) of Reg. (EU) 2018/858 on 10 Apr 2026, valid only in NL. It is an SAE Level 2 driver-assistance system; the driver stays responsible.
  • Other member states can adopt it nationally (Art. 39(5)). EU-wide validity needs a qualified majority in the TCMV: at least 15 of 27 states representing 65% of the EU population, then a Commission implementing act.
  • Slovakia: on 16 Oct 2026 the Ministry of Transport recognised the RDW approval, making it the 9th EU country (after NL, LT, EE, DK, BE, SI, CZ, HR). Tesla Europe said 'Rollout begins soon'. Minister Ráž: not a fully autonomous system, driver fully responsible. Reported by EVwire and Tesla News Wire; third-party trackers (tad-tracker.eu, fsd-eu-tracker.de) had not yet updated their counts when checked.
  • TCMV met 30 Jun and 6 Oct 2026 with only 'continuation of discussions' (no vote). Next meeting is in December, so December 2026 is the earliest possible vote. Exact December date: not published in the sources found.
  • Germany: on 6 Oct the BMV announced it had reached an agreement with Tesla in September (the system may exceed the speed limit by at most 10%; the driver remains 100% responsible) and that it will push for timely EU-wide approval. This is not a national approval. Minister Bilger said that if the EU route fails, Germany would discuss national options.
  • Tesla renamed the product 'Tesla Assisted Driving' on its European websites (reported 9 Oct 2026). Only the name changed; the approval status is the same.
  • Headwinds: Sweden's Trafikverket urged rejection unless speed-offset is removed. France rejected it 'in its current form' on 22 Jul and has been road-testing since September. A Reuters investigation (7 Oct) reported that Tesla pressured the RDW during its review.

Xpeng in Europe: markets & what is enabled
  • Xpeng was in 28 European countries as of Jan 2026: Norway (since 2021); Denmark, Sweden and the Netherlands (2023); Germany, Benelux, France, Spain and Portugal (by end 2024); Finland, Ireland and the UK (early 2025); Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Slovenia, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia (2025). On 12 Oct at the Paris Motor Show Xpeng launched the G9L (from €74,990 in France) and ran its first large-scale European NGP test rides (2 L03 in the 'Autonomous Lab', open 12–18 Oct). Xpeng says it aims to be the first automaker certified under UN R171 Series 02; that is an intention, not a certificate. No customer activation date has been given.

B · Charging & roaming

Munich court: CPO EWE Go may not charge roaming provider DCS more than its own app customers (not final)

The verdict: exactly which case

NOT FINAL
6 Oct 2026
CourtLandgericht München I (Regional Court Munich I), first instance
Case no.33 O 2062/25
DateJudgment pronounced 6 Oct 2026; written reasons not yet available (as of 7 Oct)
ClaimantDigital Charging Solutions (DCS): e-mobility service provider (EMP/MSP) behind BMW and Mercedes-Benz charging services; owned 1/3 each by BMW, Mercedes-Benz and BP (per LadeSofort)
DefendantEWE Go: charge point operator (CPO), charging subsidiary of the energy utility EWE (Oldenburg)
FiledFeb 2025; hearing Feb 2026; provisional value in dispute €700,000 (per electrive)
Legal basisAFIR (Reg. (EU) 2023/1804) Art. 5(3): no price discrimination between end users and EMPs or between EMPs, unless proportionate and objectively justified
Not this caseNo BGH, OLG or Bundeskartellamt ruling. EnBW and Ionity are NOT parties. There is no supreme-court interpretation of Art. 5(3) yet

Plain words: what was decided

  • EWE Go must stop charging DCS, in the contested form, higher prices than it charges ad-hoc customers and its own contract customers. In effect, DCS's wholesale price is capped at the €0.52 app price (electrive's reading).
  • The blocking fee charged only to MSPs is unlawful.
  • None of EWE Go's arguments justified a ~60% gap: higher admin costs, customer-service effort, business risk or customer-loyalty goals.
  • EWE Go is liable in principle for DCS's damages since 13 Apr 2024 (AFIR start). The amount will be determined later; trade press expects several million euros. EWE Go must also provide information and accounts and pay the costs.
  • The court held that AFIR's ban on discrimination applies even when the CPO sells its own app tariffs, whatever market role it acts in.

Not final: what is open

  • The judgment is not final. EWE Go is 'reviewing the reasons' (written reasons not yet published as of 16 Oct, no appeal reported). An appeal (Berufung) to the OLG München is possible; under German civil procedure the one-month deadline runs from service of the full written judgment.
  • The court did NOT decide whether the €0.27/kWh gap between the app price and the ad-hoc price (≈ +52% for card payers) is lawful.
  • It binds only EWE Go and DCS. Other CPOs (e.g. EnBW, Ionity) are not directly affected, though DCS and other EMPs can rely on the same reasoning.
  • Industry reading (CharGER via CHIP, 16 Oct): the ruling is 'not a ban on different prices' but sets a new standard for justifying them. Damages are owed from 13 Apr 2024; the amount is for a further procedure (per Dr. Web / Handelsblatt). A higher-court ruling would be needed for an EU-wide precedent (Particle summary).
Sources: electrive.net, 6 Oct 2026 (upd. 7 Oct) · ZfK, 7 Oct 2026 · LadeSofort, 6 Oct 2026 · Noerr (DCS counsel), 7 Oct 2026 · heise autos, Oct 2026 · electrive.com, 7 Oct 2026 · heise autos (EN), 7 Oct 2026 · CHIP, Oct 2026 · Dr. Web (cites Handelsblatt), Oct 2026 · Chargalytics (commentary), 9 Oct 2026
Implications for drivers & operators

Drivers

  • Nothing changes at the charger right away: the ruling is not final and covers one CPO/EMP pair.
  • If upheld, roaming (charge-card) prices could move much closer to the operators' own app prices. DCS's CEO says roaming prices could 'fall significantly'.
  • Whether EMPs pass savings on is open. AFIR Art. 5(5) separately requires EMP prices to be reasonable, transparent and non-discriminatory.
  • Observer view (not a fact): some commentators expect CPOs to respond by raising their own no-subscription app prices rather than lowering B2B prices. Trade association CharGER: 'not a ban on different prices, but a new standard for justifying them'.

Operators / EMPs

  • CPOs must be able to show objective, proportionate cost reasons for every price gap between app, ad-hoc and EMP customers.
  • There is damages exposure going back to 13 Apr 2024, plus a risk of copycat suits by other EMPs.
  • Pricing models built on 'cheap own app, expensive roaming' are now legally risky in Germany.
Sources: electrive.net, 6 Oct 2026 (upd. 7 Oct) · LadeSofort, 6 Oct 2026 · ZfK, 7 Oct 2026

When will 'overpriced' roaming surcharges end?

  • No firm date exists. AFIR's non-discrimination rule has applied since 13 Apr 2024. What was missing was case law and enforcement.
  • Step 1: does the Munich ruling become final (appeal or not)? Timing: UNCONFIRMED.
  • Step 2: a German enforcement law for AFIR price-display rules (fines up to €100,000, enforced by state price authorities) passed the Bundestag on 9 Jul 2026 and won Bundesrat consent on 25 Sep 2026, but has not yet been promulgated. Note: it covers price information and display, not price levels.
  • Step 3: from 1 Jan 2027, older (pre-13 Apr 2024) chargers of 50 kW or more on the TEN-T road network or at secure parking areas must accept card or contactless payment. That gives drivers an ad-hoc alternative to roaming at more sites.
  • Step 4: the AFIR review is due by 31 Dec 2026 (Art. 24). Price transparency, payment and idle fees are reported to be under discussion; the content of any revision is UNCONFIRMED.
Sources: Bundestagszusammenfasser (tracks Drs. 21/5873), last change 25 Sep 2026 · Deutscher Bundestag, 11 May 2026 · Elektromobilität.NRW, accessed 11 Oct 2026 · Nationale Leitstelle Ladeinfrastruktur (DE), accessed 11 Oct 2026 · European Commission DG MOVE, accessed 11 Oct 2026 · newmobility.news, 8 Oct 2026

🇨🇭 Switzerland impact

Switzerland: AFIR does not apply directly; market consolidates under JOYA

Do EU/German rules apply in Switzerland?

NO (INDIRECT)
1 Apr 2025 / 2026
  • AFIR is EU law and does not apply in Switzerland. The Munich ruling has no legal effect on Swiss CPOs or EMPs.
  • Swiss price display is governed by the Price Indication Ordinance (PBV, based on the Unfair Competition Act): prices must be clear, comparable and shown before charging, with energy priced per kWh (SECO info sheet, 1 Aug 2020).
  • Swiss Federal Office of Energy (BFE, 1 Apr 2025): AFIR affects Switzerland 'directly or indirectly' through technical standards and customer expectations. The federal government is 'checking whether action is needed' on price transparency and pricing, and will adopt AFIR rules 'where useful and compatible with Swiss law'. No concrete Swiss AFIR-style law was found as of 11 Oct 2026.
  • Switzerland already exceeds AFIR's per-vehicle charging-power targets by more than 32% (BFE, Feb 2025 data). National roads: about 58 rest areas with fast chargers by end 2025 and all 100 by 2030 (ASTRA plan, per BFE).
  • Policy now: a Federal Council consultation on a 'right to charge' for tenants and condo owners (home charging basic installation) runs until 12 Oct 2026.
Sources: SECO / via AGVS, 1 Aug 2020 · BFE / Swiss Federal Office of Energy (C. Schreyer), 1 Apr 2025 · Swiss Federal Council, 19 Jun 2026

  • Since 1 Oct 2026, Swisscharge, GOFAST, MOVE Mobility and Energie 360° Mobilität have been combined as JOYA Mobility AG (100% Energie 360°). Network: more than 2,200 own charge points plus more than 5,300 operated with partners (over 7,500). Energie 360° also cites more than 25,000 charge points incl. over 1,800 own fast-charging points and over 150,000 active users. The two counts differ, probably different scopes (UNCONFIRMED). The JOYA app is 'coming soon'. Planned investment: about CHF 150M by 2030. As of 19 Oct the JOYA site lists three plans (JOYA free, plus, max) and the JOYA app as 'coming soon', with no prices published yet; Swisscharge contracts stay unchanged for now.
  • Swisscharge roaming prices (Jan 2026, incl. VAT): MOVE AC 0.57 / DC 0.69 CHF/kWh (+0.25/min from minute 61); GOFAST DC 0.65 (+0.28/min from minute 61); IONITY 0.37 AC / 0.85 DC; Shell 0.86 / 1.02; eCarUp 0.81 / 1.19. Swisscharge states there are no extra roaming fees on top. Prices may change after the JOYA merger; check the app.
  • Tesla Superchargers CH: CHF ~0.36 (off-peak) to ~0.52/kWh (peak), varying by site (third-party aggregator, Oct 2026). Its claim that non-Teslas need a CHF 13.99/month subscription is UNVERIFIED; check the Tesla app.
  • evpass: current ad-hoc and subscription tariffs could NOT be verified (site returned an error on 11 Oct 2026).
  • Transparency is improving: the share of Swiss sessions costing more than €1/kWh fell from 25% (2024) to 9% (summer 2026), based on data from ANWB charging cards (Dutch drivers).
  • Compare live prices with the Swiss eMobility / EnergieSchweiz charge-price map.

What Swiss drivers roaming in Germany will see

ANALYSIS
11 Oct 2026
  • At German public chargers built since 13 Apr 2024 with ≥50 kW, you can pay ad-hoc with a normal debit/credit card or contactless (mobile wallet), and the €/kWh price must be shown before you start. Your bank may add a CHF→EUR currency fee.
  • From 1 Jan 2027 this also applies to older ≥50 kW chargers on the TEN-T network or at secure parking areas.
  • Ad-hoc can still cost more than the operator's own app: the Munich court did not rule on that gap. Comparing app, ad-hoc and roaming card prices before plugging in still pays off.
  • Using a Swiss card (JOYA/Swisscharge etc.) in Germany: German CPOs are bound by AFIR Art. 5(3) towards all EMPs, so if wholesale prices fall after the ruling, Swiss EMPs could benefit too. Whether Swiss EMPs are bound by Art. 5(5) (e.g. the ban on cross-border roaming surcharges) is UNCLEAR. This is our analysis, not legal advice.
  • Tesla drivers: Superchargers are unaffected by the EWE Go case. Prices are set per site in the Tesla app.
Sources: Nationale Leitstelle Ladeinfrastruktur (DE), accessed 11 Oct 2026 · Elektromobilität.NRW, accessed 11 Oct 2026 · LadeSofort, 6 Oct 2026 · electrive.net, 6 Oct 2026 (upd. 7 Oct)

Summary (follows filters)

Not in BFE list (OSM / Open Charge Map)

Separate layer, drawn like BFE stations and marked 'Not in BFE list' in the popup (checkbox above the map shows/hides it). Not part of any open-data price statistic above. 1,014 sites that are in OpenStreetMap, Open Charge Map or a hand-checked official page but have no BFE site within 75 m (150 m if the operator matches).

How: OSM amenity=charging_station (snapshot Mon 19 Oct 2026, 08:18 Berlin, clipped to the Swiss border; nodes within 30 m merged into one site): 3,709 objects → 2,928 sites; 2,155 already in BFE. Open Charge Map: 910 POIs (github export, export dated ?; partial, a free API key would give the full live set); 426 in BFE, 128 merged into an OSM site. Excluded: osm bike/scooter only 320, osm access=private 76, osm access=no 5, osm disused 1, osm access=employees 2, ocm status not operational/planned/removed 7, ocm private usage type 2, ocm licence (Oplaadpalen.nl, BY-NC-SA) 107. access=customers is kept and labelled.

Prices: official operator-website price where the operator/brand/network tag or EVSE ID matches an entry in the website-price list (dashed ring); else an OSM charge tag only if it is clearly one CHF/kWh price and the object was edited/checked in the last 2 years (also dashed ring; source named in the popup); everything else grey. Name-only or 'next to an AMAG dealer' matches show the tariff in the popup but never colour. Open Charge Map 'usage cost' text is popup-only.

Cross-check vs open data

  • M-Charge: Open data (ad-hoc, matched points): AC 0.38 (53/53), DC 50-64 kW 0.48 (58/58), 128 kW 0.55, 320 kW 0.59 - identical.
  • Move: Open data 'Ad-hoc': AC mode 0.57 (1,049 of 1,370 points), DC mode 0.69, some 0.73-0.89 - consistent with 'from' prices.
  • Fastned: Open data: 0.75 at all 72 matched points - identical.
  • Electra: Open data: CHF 0.64/kWh (Electra app tariff) at all 138 matched points = website app price 0.64; terminal price 0.69 is not in the open data.
  • Energie 360 Grad AG: Open data DC<100: 0.55/0.60/0.65 (median 0.60); DC≥100: 0.55/0.65/0.69 (median 0.65); AC 0.39-0.60 (median 0.48). Values match the website's per-site bands, but the open-data median is below the website 'standard ad-hoc' price.

Data gaps

Operators that publish no open-data price (≥10 sites, 0 priced): eCarUp (5169), Shell Recharge (450), Power Up (95), Saascharge (80), Eponet AG (77), Lidl Schweiz AG (58), Partino Mobile Energie AG (57), Plenitude On The Road (42), Tesla (36), Porsche Sales & Marketplace GmbH (20), IONITY (20), evpass (18), Chargepoint (12), 50five (12). Where the operator's own website publishes a network price, it now fills these gaps (see 'Website prices'); Tesla stays grey (prices only in the Tesla app).

Price IDs with no matching BFE station: 1,568 of 8,848 priced charge-point IDs (7,280 matched). Normalising case, separators and leading zeros found no extra matches, so these are different IDs in the two sources (e.g. M-Charge Wynecenter Buchs: BFE lists DC points CH*MIG*E*249372–249379, while the price feed only has other IDs such as …246847–246849). “(not in BFE)” = the operator prefix doesn't appear in the BFE register at all.

Inferred DC tariffs (popup only, never coloured): where an operator publishes exactly the same ad-hoc CHF/kWh at every matched DC point of a power class, unpriced DC points of that class show it as “inferred, not confirmed”: Elektrizitätswerk der Stadt Zürich 50 kW → CHF 0.60 (all 56 matched points); Fastned 300 kW → CHF 0.75 (all 48 matched points); Fastned 400 kW → CHF 0.75 (all 24 matched points); IWB Industrielle Werke Basel 100 kW → CHF 0.60 (all 12 matched points); M-Charge 50 kW → CHF 0.48 (all 50 matched points); M-Charge 128 kW → CHF 0.55 (all 60 matched points); M-Charge 320 kW → CHF 0.59 (all 26 matched points); PLUG N ROLL 50 kW → CHF 0.81 (all 10 matched points). 675 charge points get that hint.

About the data

Prices: Ladepreiskarte Swiss eMobility (via Chargeprice API charging_prices_ch, OCPI tariff elements, CHF incl. VAT; only members who publish live prices). Licence: opendata.swiss “BY ASK”, non-commercial use with attribution. 7,280 of 20,137 charge points matched to a price.

Stations: BFE ich-tanke-strom OICP feed (20,137 charge points, 9,139 sites, 41 operators; live status). Cantons from swisstopo PLZ directory.

Colour = cheapest ad-hoc (direct-payment) CHF/kWh at the site, else cheapest published CHF/kWh. Scale = 5th–95th percentile of shown sites. Time, session and parking fees are in the popup only. Errors in the source data can't be excluded.
